01
Site prep · unpacking · connections · first reagent load

Installation & Setup

The G11 is unpacked and physically installed only by a Tosoh or authorized service engineer — a service panel comes off during setup and exposes high-voltage assemblies. My job as the application specialist is everything around that: qualifying the site beforehand, verifying the unpacking checklist, making the reagent connections, and validating the system before the lab's first patient run.

Operator's Manual §2
⚠ Do not unpack or install alone

Never attempt to install, unpack, or relocate the analyzer without a Tosoh/authorized representative — even for a short in-room move. Removing the panel exposes high-voltage assemblies.

Site qualification confirm before delivery

Operating environment

Temperature15–30 °C
Humidity40–80% (no condensation)
Overvoltage categoryII
Pollution degree2
Max altitude2,000 m

Transport / storage (pre-install)

Temperature0–50 °C
Humidity≤ 80% (no condensation)
OtherKeep dry, store indoors
Operator's Manual §2.4

Avoid siting the unit where there is direct sunlight or air-conditioning draft on the analyzer, large mains fluctuations, rapid temperature swings, high dust, vibration, an unstable bench, a nearby water source (e.g. a sink), poor ventilation, or strong magnetic/RF fields. Bench must be level. Allow roughly 880 mm total height clearance above the bench (400 mm + the 480 mm unit height) and keep the rear fan and the right-side filter-handle swing path clear — the filter handle sticks out from the unit when the filter element is replaced, so leave extra space on the right when a 90SL loader is attached.

Operator's Manual §2.4

Unpacking & parts inspection

Two loader options ship separately from the main unit: 90SL (9 racks) or 290SL (29 racks). Verify contents against the packing list before the engineer leaves site.

Main unit box

  • Power cable (2 m), waste tank 10 L, waste tube 1.6 m
  • Wrenches (1/4"×5/16", 8×10 mm, hex 3 mm, 2.5 mm), screwdriver
  • 20 sample cups, printer paper roll, system USB stick
  • Reagent-pack holder, handy connector, warranty & inspection cert

Sample loader box

  • 90SL: 9 TOSOH racks · 290SL: 30 racks
  • 10 cup adapters, 2 end markers, mounting screws
  • Warranty & inspection certificate

First reagent kit

  • 1× TSKgel G11 Variant column
  • Elution Buffers No.1/2/3 (S), 800 mL×10
  • HSi Hemolysis & Wash Solution (L/LL)
  • Calibrator set + Control set
Operator's Manual §2.1

Physical connections

  1. Waste tube — insert firmly into the waste port, secure with the supplied bandage, route the other end into the 10 L waste tank. Keep the tube under 5 m, unbent, with the outlet end above the waste eluent level or the waste sensor may falsely trip and halt the run.
  2. Elution Buffer tubes — match the tube colour mark to the buffer bag: No.1 = green, No.2 = red, No.3 = yellow. Push trapped air out of each aluminium bag before sealing the cap — residual air causes degradation or poor suction.
  3. Hemolysis & Wash Solution tube — seat the anchor to the bottle bottom. If using the (LL) 4 L bottle, fit the 4 L cap and set H/W BOTTLE TYPE on the Parameter screen accordingly.
  4. Power — main switch OFF before plugging in. Requires a dedicated grounded outlet, ≥10 A, no extension cords or power strips, not shared with high-draw equipment (refrigerators, compressors).
Operator's Manual §2.5

Column & first warm-up

Let the column reach room temperature before connecting. Match the column's lot letter (A, B, …) to the same lot letter on Elution Buffers 1–3 — a lot mismatch degrades separation and can trigger persistent CALIB ERROR. Confirm the flow-direction arrow on the column label before connecting the inlet (pump side, right) and outlet (detector side, left).

  1. Power on → automatic PUMP CLEAN → BUFF PRIME → 8-minute WARMING-UP (each buffer pumped in sequence, sampling line washed twice) → STAND-BY.
  2. Confirm pump pressure sits within the initial pressure printed on the Column Inspection Report, +0 to +4 MPa.
  3. Run 3 dummy samples and review chromatogram shape before trusting results on a newly connected column.
  4. Perform a 2-point calibration, then run controls at both levels before the first patient sample.
Operator's Manual §2.6/3.3 · Guide Book §2.2

Choosing / switching analysis mode

The G11 runs one mode at a time — Variant Analysis Mode (routine HbA1c + variant screening) or β-Thalassemia Mode (F%/A2% for thalassemia screening). Switching modes means swapping the column and all three elution buffers for the other mode's dedicated set — they are not interchangeable.

  1. Bring the target mode's column and buffer pouches to room temperature.
  2. Remove the current column, cap both ends, store at 2–8 °C for later reuse. Cap and set aside the current buffers the same way.
  3. Install the new column and buffers per their IFU.
  4. On the main screen: MENU → UTILITY → MODE, select Variant or Thalassemia, SET. The system shuts down and restarts automatically.
  5. New column: run 3 dummy samples, calibrate, run QC, then proceed. Reinstalled/used column: calibrate only if maintenance was performed or assay parameters changed since its last use — otherwise run QC and proceed if it passes.
Mode-Switch Guide

02
The daily operating sequence I walk every new lab user through

Training Lab Users

This is the sequence I use when onboarding a new MT or lab tech on the G11 — from opening checks in the morning to shutdown at night. It mirrors the analyzer's own state machine, so once a user can name the states, most "what do I do now?" questions answer themselves.

Operator's Manual §3.3 · Guide Book §1

Opening checks — before pressing POWER

  • Elution Buffers 1/2/3 and Hemolysis & Wash Solution — remaining volume and expiry (never reuse or top up partially-used packs; never mix lots)
  • Printer paper — ~270 results per roll
  • Waste tank not full, waste tubing draining freely
  • USB stick has free space if results are exported
Guide Book §2.1

Power on, warm-up, log on

  1. Press POWER. Check filter/column injection counters and pump pressure as the screen comes up.
  2. Wait ~8 minutes for STAND-BY. Pressure should read within the Column Inspection Report's baseline, 0 to +4 MPa (typical system pressure ≈ 12–13 MPa). High → replace filter, then column if still high. Low → check for leaks at column/filter fittings.
  3. The User Account screen appears automatically once warm-up finishes — log on can also be done mid warm-up. Super User has full parameter access; Operator is restricted. Default password on a new login is 1234.
Guide Book §2.2–2.3
Main screen — status, pressure, countersown photo
BCR / barcode setting screenown photo

Sample preparation & required volumes

SpecimenContainerMin. volumeNote
Whole bloodPrimary tube1 mLInvert & mix before loading — non-homogeneous samples give wrong results
Whole bloodSample cup100 µLAnalyzer auto-dilutes 1:201 (default)
Pre-diluted sampleSample cup200 µLTarget dilution ≈ 1:200 (5 µL blood : 1 mL H/W); keep Total Area 600–3000
Calibrator (each level)Sample cup≥ 500 µLCal-1 injected ×3, Cal-2 injected ×2
Guide Book §2.4 · Interpretation Deck

Loading & running patients

  1. Load racks (TOSOH or SYSMEX pattern accepted) into the shaded positions; barcode label faces the reader slit. Choose rotation (needs an end-marker/empty rack at batch end) or no-rotation (up to 5 racks, right side, no end-marker needed) on the rear switch — power must be off to change it.
  2. Confirm STAND-BY, press START. First result prints in about 2 minutes; the run ends automatically when the end-marker/empty rack is detected.
  3. Analyzer runs WASH → STAND-BY → auto log-off → auto power-off (interval set under Parameter, 1/2/3 hr) if idle.
Guide Book §2.5–2.6

Calibration & QC, every day

  1. Reconstitute calibrators per their IFU (4 mL DI water each), pipette ≥500 µL into cups, load Cal-1 in rack position 1 and Cal-2 in position 2.
  2. Confirm STAND-BY, press the calibration key so CALIB: YES shows, then START. Cal-1 assays ×3, Cal-2 ×2; the mean of the 2nd+3rd Cal-1 reads and the 4th+5th Cal-2 reads sets new factors A (slope) and B (intercept). CALIB flips to COMPLETED with the date.
  3. Run controls immediately after calibration and confirm both levels sit inside their assigned range before touching a single patient sample.
Calibration factor expiry

Factors expire 30 days after the last calibration; error 153 CAL. CURVE stops the run once expired. Re-calibrate immediately after a column change, after any maintenance/repair, after a parameter change (e.g. flow factor), or whenever a control result falls outside range.

Guide Book §2.8–2.9 · Operator's Manual §3.7

STAT priority samples

Sample typeDilution keyEffective ratio
Whole bloodDECREASE1 : 401
DEFAULT1 : 201
INCREASE1 : 101
Pre-diluted—as supplied

STAT can run any time except while a prior STAT is in progress. Use it both for genuine priority samples and to re-test an AREA LOW/HIGH flagged result at an adjusted dilution.

Guide Book §2.10

What every new operator must be able to do before I sign them off

  • Read the pressure/status bar and know what STAND-BY, WARMING-UP, ANALYSIS and WASH each mean
  • Load a rack correctly and set an end-marker
  • Run a 2-point calibration and know the 30-day expiry rule
  • Run QC and recognise an out-of-range control before releasing results
  • Identify AREA LOW/HIGH and TP LOW flags on a printout and know the first corrective step
  • Replace printer paper, filter and reagents without stopping to call me
  • Know which errors to fix themselves and which need a call to the application specialist
03
Reading the chromatogram — fraction by fraction, case by case

Chromatogram Interpretation

Every G11 result is a chromatogram before it's a number. This is the section I lean on most in the field: what each of the six fractions means, what a normal trace looks like, and — case by case — what an abnormal one is telling you about the sample versus the instrument.

How the separation works

The G11 is a cation-exchange HPLC system. Hemoglobin components carry different net positive charge at the β-chain N-terminus depending on what (if anything) is attached to it. Three Elution Buffers of increasing salt concentration are pumped through the column in a 1-minute cycle, forming a salt gradient that progressively displaces bound hemoglobin from the negatively-charged resin. A blue LED detector reads absorbance at 415 nm as each fraction elutes.

Interpretation Deck, pp.3–4

The six fractions on a normal trace

Most whole-blood samples resolve into six fractions in this elution order (fastest → slowest). Real values below are from an actual G11 printout on this system.

Interpretation Deck, p.7
FractionWhat it isTypical RT
FPFast peak — earliest-eluting, least-retained material≈ 0.03–0.13
A1aPhosphorylated HbA0 derivatives (fructose-/glucose-6-phosphate adducts)≈ 0.13–0.27
A1bMinor unidentified glycated fraction≈ 0.19–0.27
FFetal hemoglobin (HbF) — normal adult reference < 2%; excluded from TOTAL AREA so it does not bias %HbA1c≈ 0.27–0.37
LA1c+Labile A1c — the reversible Schiff-base glucose adduct, a glycation precursor, not the stable fraction≈ 0.34–0.44
SA1cStable A1c — the reportable HbA1c fraction, irreversibly glycated HbA00.46–0.49 optimal
P-HV3Variant-mode only — flags the retention window where glycated HbE typically co-elutes≈ 0.44–0.60
A0Unmodified HbA0 — the dominant peak, ~90%+ of total area in a normal sample0.66–0.74 region

RT ranges for firmware 3.04+, Variant Mode, from Tosoh's official retention-time bulletin. Same-day "target" values on a specific printout (e.g. SA1c 0.46–0.48, A0 0.67–0.73) come from the calibration in effect and will drift slightly lot-to-lot — always sanity-check against your own QC chromatogram, not just this table.

Retention Time List · Operator's Manual §1.2 · Interpretation Deck
The %HbA1c calculation

%HbA1c = SA1c area ÷ (Total Area − HbF area) × 100

Because HbF is subtracted out of the denominator, elevated HbF has almost no effect on the reported %HbA1c even up to 30% HbF — the chromatogram is simply reviewed more carefully when HbF is high.

Interpretation Deck, p.3

TOTAL AREA & retention time — the concentration and calibration checks

Reading the printed report itself

Before judging any single fraction, know what's actually on the paper. A G11 report carries three blocks: an identification block (operator account, system version, sample/rack number, sample ID or barcode, calibration factor CAL(N)), a fraction table — one row per fraction with its % area, retention time (TIME) and raw area (AREA), ending in the TOTAL AREA line — and the result block, HbA1c in NGSP % and/or IFCC mmol/mol plus HbF%, printed above the chromatogram trace itself. Any flag or error text prints beneath the fraction table, immediately under the offending row.

Interpretation Deck, p.6

TOTAL AREA is a proxy for hemoglobin concentration in the diluted sample. It gates whether a result is even eligible to be reported, independent of the %HbA1c value itself.

Interpretation Deck p.36 · Operator's Manual §6.3

Walking the AREA gate with real prints

Tosoh's own deck lines up five real prints from the same sample series across the gate, which makes the shape of the failure obvious once you've seen it: at TOO LOW every fraction collapses toward zero and the chromatogram is nearly flat; through LOW→recommended→HIGH the trace simply gets taller while HbA1c%/IFCC/HbF stay the *same* (9.8% / 84 / ~1.2–1.3% across all three middle prints — proof the ratio-based %HbA1c calculation is stable across a 6× concentration swing); at TOO HIGH the report withholds HbA1c/IFCC/HbF entirely (blank fields, not a wrong number).

ZoneTOTAL AREAReal example (A0 row)Action
TOO LOW< 500A0 366.7 / TOTAL 421.2 — HbA1c withheldNot reportable. Re-cup and STAT-INCREASE, or check H&W supply / needle.
LOW500–600A0 478.4 / TOTAL 549.3 — HbA1c 9.8%Reportable, but re-test if volume was marginal.
recommended600–3000A0 913.6 / TOTAL 992.9 — HbA1c 5.4%Report as-is.
HIGH3000–3500A0 2727.6 / TOTAL 3135.1 — HbA1c 9.8%Reportable; watch for carry-over into the next samples.
TOO HIGH> 3500A0 3315.6 / TOTAL 3811.2 — HbA1c withheldNot reportable. Mix/re-centrifuge check, STAT-DECREASE, or verify not an analyzer fault.

Exact figures traced from the Interpretation deck's real printouts (TOTAL AREA / TP LOW / AREA LOW / AREA HIGH walkthrough slides).

Interpretation Deck, pp.11–13
AREA TOO LOW that repeats on every sample — insufficient suction, not the patient

If TOTAL AREA collapses on run after run (not just one patient), the cause is almost always mechanical: hemolysis & wash (H/W) solution running low, H/W tubing kinked or lifted out of the bottle, or a clogged sampling needle. Air trapped in the H/W line trips error "146 H/W EMPTY" specifically. Check the bottle level and tubing before opening a service ticket.

Interpretation Deck, p.14

Retention time — target windows and what moves them

Target RT on this instrument: SA1c 0.46–0.48 min, A0 0.67–0.73 min. A trace that lands outside this window is redrawn wider (broadened) or shifted, and the analyzer may mis-assign which peak is SA1c — the report then either substitutes the wrong peak into the calculation or throws SA1C NOT DETECT.

RT of A0 longer than usual
  • Leak at a filter or column fitting — tighten the connection
  • Clogged suction filter — replace
  • Air trapped in the pump — run Drain Flush
RT of A0 shorter than usual
  • Elution Buffer opened > 3 months ago — replace with fresh pouches
  • Elution Buffer not capped tightly after opening — check the seal, replace if suspect
Interpretation Deck, pp.16–17

Elution buffer bottles swapped — a distinct RT fingerprint

Buffers No.1/No.2/No.3 (green/red/amber tube colour) feed the gradient in a fixed low→high salt order. Connect two bottles to the wrong ports and every fraction's RT shifts together in a recognisable pattern rather than randomly — worth checking tube colour against the port label before assuming a pump fault.

Interpretation Deck, p.18

Three checks on every result before you trust it

  1. Flags / errors — nothing printed in the flag line, and no error message.
  2. Retention times — SA1c and A0 both sit in their target window; a shift usually points at the instrument (buffer, filter, pump) rather than the patient.
  3. TOTAL AREA — inside 600–3000 (recommended); outside 500–3500 the value is not reportable at all.
Interpretation Deck, pp.7–8

Does the number make clinical sense?

A chromatogram can be flag-free, in-range on RT, and in-range on TOTAL AREA, and still be wrong for the patient. HbA1c reflects roughly the preceding 8–12 weeks of average glucose, so it lags a fasting glucose reading by weeks — the two numbers are not meant to match on the same day, but they should track the same general direction over a patient's history. When they clearly don't, that's a second, independent reason to suspect a variant even with a "clean" trace.

HbA1c% reading low for the patient's glucose
  • Check for anemia, kidney failure, or liver disease — shortened red-cell lifespan lowers HbA1c independent of glycemic control
  • Check for blood-forming medication — new (less-glycated) red cells raised in proportion, lowering HbA1c
  • If neither applies: possible hemoglobin variant — do not report
HbA1c% reading high for the patient's glucose
  • Genuinely poor glycemic control is still the most common explanation — correlate with the chart
  • If glucose and HbA1c disagree with no clinical explanation: possible hemoglobin variant — do not report
Interpretation Deck, pp.20–22

Tosoh validated the underlying math with a mixing-recovery study — blending a high-HbA1c and a low-HbA1c sample in known ratios and comparing the measured result against the theoretical blend. Recovery held at 100–103% across the full 2.7–20.1% range, confirming that as long as the SA1c fraction is correctly separated and identified, %HbA1c is essentially linear from 0–100% — useful context when a clinician questions whether a result "can really be that high or that low."

Interpretation Deck, p.23
A related check — is the calibration factor plausible?

CAL(N) prints in the identification block of every report. A sudden jump in CAL(N) between calibrations, without a matching column or buffer lot change, is worth a second look before trusting the batch of results that follow it — see the calibration procedure in §05.

Case-by-case gallery

The single most useful habit I teach: ask "is it only this sample, or is it every sample?" One bad sample points at the patient or the specimen; every sample going bad at once points at the analyzer.

Sample-related vs analyzer-related
Only one specific sample
→ stir/re-mix, adjust dilution, cross-check other lab results, consider a variant
Almost every sample
→ replace filter/column, check reagent lot match, re-prime, re-calibrate, service call
Interpretation Deck, p.9
Normal chromatogramReportable
Pattern

No flag/error, all six fractions correctly identified, SA1c & A0 RT in range, TOTAL AREA 600–3000.

Action

Report as-is.

AREA LOW / AREA TOO LOWReportable ≥500, not below
Pattern

TOTAL AREA < 600 (LOW) or < 500 (TOO LOW — do not report). Below 100, expect missing-peak flags too.

Likely cause & action

Low hemoglobin concentration (dialysis, anemia) or insufficient sample volume — re-run via STAT with INCREASE dilution, or manually dilute and re-cup. If it affects every sample: check H/W solution level, tubing, and needle for clogging.

AREA HIGH / AREA TOO HIGHReportable ≤3500, not above
Pattern

TOTAL AREA > 3000 (HIGH) or > 3500 (TOO HIGH — do not report).

Likely cause & action

Centrifuged/sedimented or highly concentrated sample — mix and re-assay, or STAT with DECREASE dilution. Extremely high area (>10,000) risks carryover into the next 10 results — see the recovery procedure in §06.

TP LOW / TP TOO LOWDepends on pattern
Pattern

SA1c peak shape has broadened (theoretical plate count below 300, or 0).

Likely cause & action

If every sample shows it — the column is degrading, plan replacement. If it's one specific sample — suspect a hemoglobin variant.

Inappropriate retention time (shorter / longer than target)
RT of A0 longer than usual

Leak at filter/column fitting (tighten), clogged suction filter (replace), or air trapped in the pump — try Drain Flush.

RT of A0 shorter than usual

Elution Buffer opened > 90 days ago, or not capped tightly after opening — replace with fresh pouches, verify seal.

All RTs shift together

A specific buffer pair may be cross-connected: No.1↔2 swapped, No.1↔3 swapped, or No.2↔3 swapped each give a distinct RT-shift signature — check the tube colour against the bag label (green/red/yellow) before assuming a mechanical fault.

Consequence

SA1c may not be correctly identified; an unidentified peak between SA1c and A0 (flag PXX) or a missing-peak flag can appear.

Interpretation Deck, pp.16–18
Elevated HbFReportable — HbA1c unaffected up to 30% HbF
Pattern

HbF% above the <2% adult reference; may co-elute with LA1c+ (flag LA1C+ NOT DETECT) or with A1a (A1B NOT DETECT). Real example: F fraction 12.87 area, HbF flagged, UNKNOWN PEAK / HBF SUSPECTED printed — HbA1c still calculated at 4.6%.

Why it doesn't distort %HbA1c

HbF is developmentally the dominant hemoglobin before birth and is normally almost fully replaced by adult HbA0 within the first two years of life; a level still elevated in an adult sample (thalassemia, hereditary persistence of HbF, some hematologic conditions) simply widens the F peak. Because HbF area is subtracted out of the %HbA1c denominator (SA1c ÷ (Total Area − HbF)), Tosoh's spiked-recovery study shows ~100% recovery up to 30% HbF — no correction needed, just confirm the SA1c peak itself wasn't swallowed by the F or LA1c+ shoulder.

Interpretation Deck, pp.24–26, 35
Large A1a peakUsually reportable
Pattern

A1a fraction abnormally large (real example: A1A 13.53 area vs. a normal ≈5) with an intact, correctly-timed SA1c peak elsewhere in the trace.

Likely cause & action

Usually excess blood-plasma carryover in the sample — HPLC is not interfered by plasma, so it's still reportable as-is. If the peak is still abnormally large after re-drawing/confirming plasma wasn't the cause, suspect a hemoglobin variant (flag A1A NOT DETECT may also appear) and do not report.

Interpretation Deck, p.27
Aged / deteriorated sampleNot reportable
Pattern

Broadened, distorted, or extra abnormal peaks versus a fresh draw from the same patient — LA1c+ and A1a areas inflate noticeably as the sample sits.

Action

Request a fresh sample. Whole blood is stable 14 days refrigerated (any of EDTA-2Na/2K/3K, heparin Na/Li, or NaF+citric-acid+EDTA combinations — no meaningful HbA1c difference between anticoagulants) or 24 h at room temperature; beyond that, treat results with suspicion.

Interpretation Deck, pp.28–29
Centrifuged / settled sampleMix before assay
Pattern

A HbA1c gradient exists across the settled cell layer under strong centrifugation or long standing — older RBCs (higher glycation, more time to accumulate SA1c) sink toward the bottom, newer cells (lower glycation) stay nearer the plasma — so the result depends on exactly where the sampling needle drew from.

Action

Always invert/stir before loading, especially for anemia and dialysis patients where this effect is most pronounced (mixed red-cell ages, frequent transfusion or altered erythropoiesis).

Interpretation Deck, p.31
Chemically modified hemoglobins — labile A1c, carbamylated Hb, acetaldehyde Hb

These are not genetic variants — glucose, urea (renal failure), or aldehydes attach to hemoglobin chemically and can confound immunoassay/boronate methods. Tosoh's own spiking studies (glucose up to 1000 mg/dL, sodium cyanate up to 25 mmol/L, acetaldehyde up to 25 mmol/L) plot LA1c+% rising sharply with each spiked interferent while SA1c% stays essentially flat across the whole range — because HPLC physically separates the labile/carbamylated/aldehyde adducts into the LA1c+ fraction rather than co-eluting them with SA1c. A real chromatogram of spiked aldehyde hemoglobin shows the extra peak appearing well before SA1c, never overlapping it.

Interpretation Deck p.30 · Performance Data (Variant)
Analyzer-caused abnormal patterns (affects a run of consecutive samples)
Symptom

No-good / distorted chromatogram across samples

Peak detection errors, missing peaks

TOTAL AREA very low across the run

Likely cause

Column deterioration

Defective pump delivery, air in line

Insufficient sample suction / H&W solution empty

Guide Book §4.4 · Operator's Manual §6.4
Column Inspection Report — real traceown photo

Hemoglobin variants

Hemoglobin variants are inherited amino-acid substitutions in the globin chains — over 700 forms are documented, most as single substitutions in the β-chain. People carry them from birth, often with no symptoms; some (HbS, HbC, HbE, HbD) are common enough in Southeast Asian and Mediterranean populations that an Application Specialist in Thailand will see them regularly. A few, like the sickle disorders (HbSS, HbSC, HbS/β-thal), are clinically serious in their own right.

Interpretation Deck, p.32

Because a variant hemoglobin carries a different net charge than HbA, its elution position — and its glycated form's position — shift away from the normal A0/A1c windows. Three patterns follow:

Pattern 1 — Unknown peak

Variant peak elutes clear of both A0 and A1c. Typical of HbAE, HbAS, HbAC, HbAD. SA1c% is usually still valid — reportable.

Pattern 2 — Overlap

Variant's glycated form co-elutes with SA1c, falsely elevating the reported %. Not reportable without confirmation.

Pattern 3 — Unknown peak

Same signature as Pattern 1, seen with HbAS, HbAC, HbAD heterozygotes — usually reportable.

Interpretation Deck, pp.33–34
Variant traitG11 Variant Mode — HbA1c interference?
HbC traitYes — interferes
HbS traitNo interference
HbE traitNo interference
HbD traitNo interference

NGSP's independently-tested interference table for "Tosoh G11 Variant Mode." Homozygous states (HbSS, HbCC, HbSC) and double heterozygotes have no normal HbA present at all — HbA1c cannot be used for glycemic monitoring regardless of method; switch to glycated albumin/fructosamine.

NGSP Interference Table, updated 2019-04-19

Finding a variant when the chromatogram looks fine

Not every variant announces itself with an abnormal peak. If a specific sample's %HbA1c doesn't track with the patient's blood-glucose trend, work through this before concluding "variant":

  1. Rule out short RBC lifespan: anemia, deteriorating kidney function, liver cirrhosis — these lower measured HbA1c without any chromatogram abnormality. Switch to an alternative glycemic marker for these patients.
  2. Rule out treatment effects: anemia therapy raising the proportion of new (less glycated) red cells — same fix, switch methods.
  3. If neither applies, a hemoglobin variant is the remaining explanation.
Interpretation Deck, pp.37–38
What to report to the clinician for a suspected variant
  • Do not report the HPLC HbA1c value.
  • Re-test to confirm the abnormality is patient-related, not instrument-related.
  • Recommend an alternative glycemic test — immunoassay or boronate affinity — and report that value only if it matches what's expected from the glucose trend.
  • Flag relevant clinical context (CBC morphology, biochemistry) for the clinician.
  • Definitive variant typing needs DNA analysis — HPLC alone cannot identify which variant is present, only that one is likely there; the chromatogram plus a complete blood count go together to the specialist who requests it.
Interpretation Deck, p.39

Why HPLC is still the right front-line method for variant screening

No single method both measures HbA1c and detects variants cleanly — the point of HPLC on the G11 is that it does the detection half well, even where it can't safely do the measurement half.

HPLC (G11)Immunoassay / Boronate Affinity
HbA1c% measurement✗ should not be reported (variant present)△ affected by some variants too
Hemoglobin variant detection○ abnormal chromatogram pattern visible✗ no additional information to HbA1c%
Preventive function against a wrong report○ flag & error messages notify abnormal chromatograms✗ none

This is exactly why the G11's flag system matters operationally: it's the thing standing between an unnoticed variant and a wrong number reaching a clinician.

Interpretation Deck, p.40

β-Thalassemia Mode — reading F% / A2%

In β-Thal mode the same cation-exchange principle separates HbF and HbA2 instead of HbA1c fractions, in about 5 minutes per sample. A β-thalassemia trait pattern shows HbA2 elevated above the normal adult range, sometimes with HbF also raised.

AnalyteTarget RT (G11)WHO/NIBSC traceability
HbF0.58–0.64 optimalNIBSC 85/616, assigned 3.4%
HbA22.16–2.32 optimalNIBSC 89/666, assigned 5.3%

Reported precision: intra-assay CV 0.4–1.9% and inter-assay CV 0.6–1.9% across low/high controls; no interference from HbE, HbD, HbS or HbC; detects HbF up to 50%; 2-point calibration, same as Variant mode. Switching between Variant and β-Thal mode follows the column/buffer swap procedure in §01.

β-Thal Presentation · β-Thal Performance Data · Retention Time List

Codes 2/30/35/42/45 were read directly off a configured Thai-market unit's FLAG parameter screens (P.01–P.03) and may vary by site configuration — always confirm against the live FLAG screen on the instrument in front of you, not this table alone.

Interpretation Deck p.36 · Operator's Manual §4.21 · own photos

The flag line is not decoration — it's the instrument actively warning you before a bad number gets reported. Two real examples: an UNKNOWN PEAK co-eluting near where HbF would be, flagged HBF SUSPECTED, on an otherwise normal-looking 4.6% trace; and a broadened SA1c peak flagged TP LOW on a second sample where the peak shape — not its position — is what's wrong.

04
Who does what, on what schedule

Maintenance

Maintenance on the G11 splits cleanly into three tiers: what the operator does every day, what the operator replaces on a schedule, and what's reserved for a service engineer. Knowing the boundary is most of the job — it tells a lab user when to keep going and when to call me.

Daily care

Wipe plastic housings (needle cover etc.) with a soft cloth and neutral detergent — never organic solvents on plastic, they warp and discolour it. Metal parts can take ethanol for stubborn dirt; dry them afterward to prevent rust. Lightly wipe the loader belt, display and keys with ethanol.

Operator's Manual §5.1

Operator's Manual §5.2 · Guide Book §3.1–3.2

Replace the column when…

  • Pressure exceeds baseline +4 MPa and doesn't drop after a filter change
  • Chromatograms show unknown peaks (P00–PXX) or fewer than 6 peaks
  • QC results sit outside their assigned range even after re-calibration
  • CALIB ERROR recurs frequently
  • The expiration date on the label has passed
Operator's Manual §5.9 · Guide Book §3.2

Pre-assay daily checklist

  • Calibration settings — factor and date current (≤30 days)
  • Column — injection counter and expiry
  • Filter — injection counter
  • Elution Buffers — remaining volume and expiry
  • Hemolysis & Wash Solution — remaining volume and expiry
  • USB stick — remaining capacity
  • Printer paper — remaining roll
  • Waste tank — not full

Calibrator box — storage labelown photo
Control vials, Level 1 & 2own photo

Long-term shutdown (> 1 week idle)

  1. Remove the column, cap both ends with the original plugs, refrigerate at 4–15 °C.
  2. Connect the union (P/N 0006163) in place of the column.
  3. Move all Elution Buffer and H&W suction tubes into a bottle of purified water; seal the actual reagent packs for reuse later.
  4. Prime all lines with purified water via the REAGENT CHANGE screen.
  5. Run COLUMN WASH to flush all lines through with water.
Never cross-wash the lines

Do not wash the Hemolysis & Wash Solution line with Elution Buffer, and never insert the Elution Buffer suction tube into H&W Solution to "clean" it.

Operator's Manual §6.1

Condensed replacement procedures

Filter (every 600 injections)

  1. Confirm STAND-BY, open the door below the display.
  2. Turn the filter handle counter-clockwise (open), pull the holder, discard the old element as biohazard.
  3. Seat a new element (flange = outlet, upward), re-insert the holder, turn the handle clockwise until it stops.
  4. Run COLUMN WASH, confirm pressure back within baseline +4 MPa.
  5. Reset the filter counter on the REAGENT CHANGE screen.

Column

  1. Bring the new column to room temperature ~30 min first; confirm STAND-BY.
  2. Open the column oven, remove the old column, unplug protective caps from the new one.
  3. Connect inlet (pump/right side) first, flow-check, then connect outlet (detector/left side) — flow arrow points right→left.
  4. Run COLUMN WASH, then verify pressure and run 3 dummy samples before calibrating.
  5. Reset the column counter; calibrate; run QC.
Operator's Manual §5.8–5.9 · Guide Book §3.1–3.2

Buffer/H&W replacement, buffer priming, pump air removal (drain flush) and printer paper are all one-touch procedures from the MAINTE screen — the guided on-screen prompts walk the operator through each; my role during training is to run each one once with the operator watching, then have them repeat it back to me.

Biohazard handling

The filter, column and sampling needle all contact patient blood. Wear goggles, gloves and a mask during replacement, and dispose of used parts as infectious waste per your facility's SOP.

05
Calibration discipline, QC data, and host connectivity

Performance & QC Workflow

When calibration is mandatory

  • Control value falls outside its assigned range
  • After every column replacement
  • After maintenance or repair (plunger seal, etc.)
  • After any assay-parameter change (e.g. flow factor)
  • Calibration factors have expired — 30 days after the last calibration

The CALIB indicator on the main screen reads YES (will auto-calibrate before the next run), COMPLETED (calibration applied, date shown), or NO (assay uses the currently stored factors A/B without recalibrating). Aligned values can be entered manually in NGSP% or IFCC mmol/mol, or scanned automatically from the calibrator's barcode sheet with the handy scanner.

Operator's Manual §3.7

QC discipline

Run control material every day, at two levels (normal + abnormal) minimum, and always immediately after calibration before releasing any patient result. Each lab should establish its own reference interval appropriate to the population served — never rely on the analyzer's raw output as a clinical cutoff on its own.

Performance Data (β-Thal)

Data management & recalculation

The analyzer holds the last 800 results internally (oldest overwritten first); export to USB for longer retention. Any stored result — internal memory or USB — can be re-printed, re-transmitted to the host, or recalculated against updated calibration factors from the RECALC screen, without re-running the sample.

Operator's Manual §2.3/§4.12 · Guide Book §4.1–4.2

LIS / host connectivity

Since I'm also looking at LIS specialist roles, this is the part of the workflow I pay closest attention to. The G11 talks to a host over RS-232C, bi-directional, half-duplex, using an ASTM/CLSI-style record structure — the same lineage of protocol used across most mid-size analyzer↔LIS interfaces.

ParameterValue
Lower-level protocolCLSI LIS1-A2 (ASTM E1381-91)
Physical layerRS-232C, asynchronous, half-duplex
Baud rate1200 / 2400 / 4800 / 9600 / 19200 / 38400 bps
Data / parity / stop bit7 or 8 bit · even/odd/none · 1 or 2 bit
ConnectorD-SUB 9-pin (socket) on the instrument side

Higher-level messages are built from tagged records — H (message header), P (patient info), O (test order), R (result/concentration), C (instrument flag comment), Q (request/query), S (scientific), M (manufacturer info), L (terminator) — used for batch host queries, single-specimen queries, and result transmission. In query mode the analyzer only runs samples the host has actually ordered by barcode; in error-skip mode an unreadable barcode causes that sample to be skipped rather than halting the run.

Host Comm. Spec (Piano Evo-4/501RP+) · Operator's Manual §4.20
HOST LOG VIEW — live message trafficown photo

The Log View screen (Main → Menu → Log File Check) is the fastest way to confirm whether a "sample not sent to LIS" complaint is an instrument-side transmission failure or a host-side rejection — read the raw record before escalating either way.

Operator's Manual §6.3

Drain Flush — recovering from PRESSURE LOW

  1. Confirm sufficient Elution Buffer remains before starting.
  2. Open the door on the left side; turn the drain valve 90° counter-clockwise (never more) to open.
  3. Follow the on-screen DRAIN VALVE prompts to run the flush (~4 minutes).
  4. Close the drain valve — turn 90° clockwise back to closed.
  5. Run COLUMN WASH; confirm pressure has returned to baseline — that confirms the air is out.
Guide Book, Appendix-3

Recovering from an extreme AREA TOO HIGH (>10,000)

Carryover risk: treat the flagged sample and the next 10 consecutive results as unreliable.

  1. Replace the filter.
  2. Load 5–10 sample cups with 1 mL purified water each on a rack.
  3. Run them until a 200 AREA LOW ERROR with TOTAL AREA < 50 appears three times in a row — the analyzer then enters WASH automatically. Remove the rack.
  4. Power off, then power back on.
  5. Calibrate, confirm QC passes, then re-measure the affected samples.
Operator's Manual §6.5

Power interruptions

Planned outage

  1. Save parameters to USB, remove the stick
  2. Print the parameter list as a backup record
  3. Switch off the main power

Unplanned outage

  1. Do not touch any sample tube or cup mid-run
  2. When power returns, switch the main power back on and let the system re-initialize
Operator's Manual §6.6 · Guide Book Appendix-4
Liquid leak — stop first, diagnose second

Switch off immediately and unplug on any leak — treat it as blood-contaminated waste and wear PPE. A leak at the column connection trips the column leak sensor and halts the assay automatically; wipe the area and reseat the column. If the source isn't obvious or won't stop, call Tosoh/the local representative rather than continuing to troubleshoot live.
